{{< new-terms >}}

## Survey effort leaves conditions a model has never seen

Survey effort is never spread evenly over the sea. It follows ports, weather, ship time
and the questions of the day, so some conditions are sampled hundreds of times and
others never. **Uneven sampling** means some conditions are covered thinly, so a
model's fit there rests on a few stations. **Extrapolation** means predicting for
conditions the survey did not cover at all. A model still answers there, and nothing in
the answer shows that it is guessing.

Each method carries on past the data in its own way. Linear regression keeps its slope,
polynomial regression follows its curve wherever the bend takes it, and decision trees,
random forests and k-nearest neighbours level off at the edge of the data;
[Choosing a method](../03-supervised-learning/choosing-a-method.qmd#beyond-the-sampled-temperatures-each-model-follows-its-own-rule)
draws three of them side by side. This page checks two of them against the truth past
the data, and measures how far a station lies from the survey, so that a prediction map
can say where it is guessing.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## The distance to the nearest surveyed station shows where a model is guessing

The usual check takes each input in turn and asks whether a station's value lies
between the smallest and largest the survey recorded. It misses a station that is
inside every range but in a combination of conditions the survey never met, such as
shallow water as cold as the survey found only at depth.

A check that looks at all the inputs together measures the **distance to the nearest
surveyed station**: the distance [k-nearest neighbours](../03-supervised-learning/nearest-neighbours.qmd)
uses to find its neighbours, with the inputs standardised so that each counts alike. A
station far from every surveyed station is one the model knows little about, whatever
each input says alone. Conditions the survey covered thinly lie further from their
nearest station too, so the same distance shows uneven sampling.

::: {.diagram}
![A range check takes each input alone, so a shallow, cold station passes because its depth and its temperature each lie inside the survey's range. The distance to the nearest surveyed station takes all the inputs together and flags it, because the survey never met shallow, cold water.](img/range-and-distance.svg){fig-alt="Two cards, each a chart of depth across and temperature down on which the surveyed stations form a band from warm, shallow water to cold, deep water. Range check, each input alone: a dashed box spans the survey's range of depth and of temperature, and a new shallow, cold station sits inside it, so it passes. Distance to the survey, all inputs together: a line joins the same station to its nearest surveyed station across empty space, so it is flagged as far; a second new station inside the band has a short line and is close. A note says the inputs are standardised first, as for k-nearest neighbours."}
:::

## Worked example

The survey here visits only the shallower sites: those whose stations average less
than 100 m deep. The deeper sites are the area the model is asked to map. Two methods
are fitted with the same inputs: polynomial regression from
[Linear and polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd),
with squared terms for depth and temperature, and the random forest from
[Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd).

One survey could be lucky or unlucky, so the fit is repeated on ten surveys, each
made of a different three quarters of the shallow sites. The quarter left out each
time gives new sites within the survey's depths, to set against the deep sites. The
last two parts turn to a survey that sailed only in summer and autumn.

### Preparing the data

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |>
  mutate(site_depth = mean(depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), .by = site_id)

shallow <- filter(survey, site_depth < 100)
deep <- filter(survey, site_depth >= 100)

# ten surveys, each of three quarters of the shallow sites
surveys <- group_mc_cv(shallow, group = site_id, prop = 0.75, times = 10)

forest_recipe <- recipe(
  abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu +
    substrate + season,
  data = shallow
) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand")

curve_recipe <- forest_recipe |>
  step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import (OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures,
                                   StandardScaler)

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean, load_coastal_survey_truth

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()
survey["site_depth"] = survey.groupby("site_id")["depth_m"].transform("mean")

shallow = survey[survey["site_depth"] < 100].reset_index(drop=True)
deep = survey[survey["site_depth"] >= 100].reset_index(drop=True)

# ten surveys, each of three quarters of the shallow sites
surveys = list(GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=10, train_size=0.75, random_state=123)
               .split(shallow, groups=shallow["site_id"]))

categorical = ["substrate", "season"]
predictors = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3",
              "salinity_psu"] + categorical

def squared(column):
    return (column, Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)),
    ]), [column])

curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    squared("depth_m"),
    squared("temperature_c"),
    ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
     ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]),
    ("categorical",
     OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False),
     categorical),
])

forest_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), predictors[:4]),
    ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical),
])
```

:::

The survey has `r n_distinct(shallow$site_id)` of the `r n_distinct(survey$site_id)`
sites. The other `r n_distinct(deep$site_id)` sites, down to
`r round(max(deep$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE))` m, are the area to map.

### Methods that agree within the survey's depths disagree below them

Each of the ten surveys fits both methods, which then predict every station at
the left-out shallow sites and at the deep sites.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fits
predict_two <- \(one_survey) {
  fitting <- analysis(one_survey)
  new_sites <- bind_rows(assessment(one_survey), deep)

  polynomial <- fit(workflow(curve_recipe, linear_reg()), fitting)
  forest <- fit(
    workflow(forest_recipe,
             rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
               set_engine("ranger") |>
               set_mode("regression")),
    fitting
  )

  new_sites |>
    select(station_id, site_id, depth_m) |>
    mutate(
      "Polynomial regression" = predict(polynomial, new_sites)$.pred,
      "Random forest" = predict(forest, new_sites)$.pred
    )
}

predictions <- surveys |>
  mutate(predicted = map(splits, predict_two)) |>
  select(id, predicted) |>
  unnest(predicted) |>
  pivot_longer(c("Polynomial regression", "Random forest"),
               names_to = "model", values_to = "predicted")
```

## Python

```{python}
def predict_two(fit_rows, held_rows):
    fitting = shallow.iloc[fit_rows]
    new_sites = pd.concat([shallow.iloc[held_rows], deep], ignore_index=True)

    polynomial = Pipeline([("recipe", curve_recipe),
                           ("model", LinearRegression())]).fit(
        fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"])
    forest = Pipeline([
        ("recipe", forest_recipe),
        ("model", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, random_state=1,
                                        n_jobs=-1)),
    ]).fit(fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"])

    return new_sites[["station_id", "site_id", "depth_m"]].assign(
        **{"Polynomial regression": polynomial.predict(new_sites[predictors]),
           "Random forest": forest.predict(new_sites[predictors])})

predictions = pd.concat(
    [predict_two(fit_rows, held_rows).assign(id=i)
     for i, (fit_rows, held_rows) in enumerate(surveys)]
).melt(id_vars=["id", "station_id", "site_id", "depth_m"],
       var_name="model", value_name="predicted")
```

:::

The survey is simulated, so the predictions can be compared with the **true mean
count** at each station: the number the simulation drew that station's count around.
No real study has this; it shows each method's error free of the noise in single
counts.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: truth
predictions <- predictions |>
  left_join(load_coastal_survey_truth(), by = "station_id")
```

## Python

```{python}
predictions = predictions.merge(load_coastal_survey_truth(), on="station_id")
```

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-beyond
#| fig-cap: "Mean predicted count at new sites in 20 m bands of depth, one thin line for each of the ten shallow surveys, against the true mean count (black). The shaded region holds the depths of the sites the surveys left out. Within the survey's depths the ten fits of each method agree with each other and with the truth. Below them the random forest's lines run flat, and polynomial regression's lines fan out."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels, one per method, each with depth from 20 to 180 metres on the horizontal axis and mean count on the vertical, with the region deeper than 100 metres shaded. A thick black line for the true mean count falls from about 7 at 30 metres to about 4 at 90 metres, stays near 3.5 to 120 metres and then drops to about 1 at 170 metres. In every panel the ten thin blue lines bunch around the black line up to 100 metres. Beyond it: for polynomial regression the thin lines spread out, some following the black line down, others staying level or turning upward; for the random forest all ten lines stay level between about 3 and 5, well above the black line at the deepest bands."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
bands <- predictions |>
  filter(between(depth_m, 20, 180)) |>
  mutate(depth = 20 * floor(depth_m / 20) + 10)

truth_line <- bands |>
  summarise(true_mean = mean(true_mean), .by = c(model, depth))

bands |>
  summarise(predicted = mean(predicted), .by = c(model, id, depth)) |>
  ggplot(aes(depth, predicted)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 100, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey92") +
  geom_line(aes(group = id), colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_line(aes(y = true_mean), data = truth_line, linewidth = 1.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Mean count (individuals)")
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: ratios
#| include: false
ratios <- predictions |>
  mutate(where = case_when(
    site_id %in% shallow$site_id ~ "within",
    depth_m > 140 ~ "below"
  )) |>
  filter(!is.na(where)) |>
  summarise(ratio = mean(predicted) / mean(true_mean),
            .by = c(model, id, where))
spread_of <- \(m, w) {
  r <- range(ratios$ratio[ratios$model == m & ratios$where == w])
  paste(format(round(r, 1), nsmall = 1), collapse = " to ")
}
```

Within the survey's depths, @fig-beyond shows the ten fits of each method bunched
around the truth. Past 100 m they part company. The random forest's lines run flat:
it predicts a station at 170 m much as it predicts one at the deepest point of its
survey, while the true mean count keeps falling. Below 140 m it is too high on all ten
surveys, at `r spread_of("Random forest", "below")` times the truth. Polynomial
regression's lines fan out instead, from `r spread_of("Polynomial regression", "below")`
times the truth: within 100 m the water gets colder as it gets deeper, so fits that
describe the shallow sites equally well can bend in different directions below them.

### Shallow, cold stations pass a range check but lie far from the survey

Spotting that 170 m lies beyond a survey of sites shallower than 100 m is easy. A new
combination is harder. Suppose a survey sailed only in summer and autumn, and its
model is asked about spring and winter stations. The distance uses the four measured
inputs, standardised as in [Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd)
with chlorophyll logged first. A station is flagged as far from the survey when it lies
further from it than 95% of surveyed stations lie from their nearest neighbour at
another site (at another site, because a site's own visits sit close together).

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: distance
surveyed <- filter(survey, season %in% c("summer", "autumn"))
asked <- filter(survey, season %in% c("spring", "winter"))
inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu")

distance_recipe <- recipe(surveyed[inputs]) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric()) |>
  step_log(chlorophyll_mg_m3) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric()) |>
  prep()
surveyed_scaled <- as.matrix(bake(distance_recipe, new_data = NULL))
asked_scaled <- as.matrix(bake(distance_recipe, asked))

# distance from each row of `from` to the nearest row of `to`
nearest <- \(from, to) {
  apply(from, 1, \(row) min(sqrt(colSums((t(to) - row)^2))))
}

# how far each surveyed station lies from the nearest at another site
neighbour_gap <- map_dbl(seq_len(nrow(surveyed)), \(i) {
  other_sites <- surveyed$site_id != surveyed$site_id[i]
  nearest(surveyed_scaled[i, , drop = FALSE], surveyed_scaled[other_sites, ])
})
limit <- quantile(neighbour_gap, 0.95)

in_range <- \(column) {
  seen <- range(surveyed[[column]], na.rm = TRUE)
  is.na(asked[[column]]) | between(asked[[column]], seen[1], seen[2])
}

asked <- asked |>
  mutate(distance = nearest(asked_scaled, surveyed_scaled),
         far = distance > limit,
         every_range = reduce(map(inputs, in_range), `&`))

asked |>
  summarise(stations = n(),
            `inside every range` = sum(every_range),
            `far from the survey` = sum(far),
            `inside every range but far` = sum(every_range & far))
```

## Python

```{python}
surveyed = survey[survey["season"].isin(["summer", "autumn"])].reset_index(drop=True)
asked = survey[survey["season"].isin(["spring", "winter"])].reset_index(drop=True)
inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]

def logged(frame):
    return frame[inputs].assign(
        chlorophyll_mg_m3=np.log(frame["chlorophyll_mg_m3"]))

distance_recipe = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
]).fit(logged(surveyed))
surveyed_scaled = distance_recipe.transform(logged(surveyed))
asked_scaled = distance_recipe.transform(logged(asked))

# how far each surveyed station lies from the nearest at another site
gaps = cdist(surveyed_scaled, surveyed_scaled)
same_site = surveyed["site_id"].to_numpy()[:, None] == surveyed["site_id"].to_numpy()
gaps[same_site] = np.inf
limit = np.quantile(gaps.min(axis=1), 0.95)

def in_range(column):
    low, high = surveyed[column].min(), surveyed[column].max()
    return asked[column].isna() | asked[column].between(low, high)

asked["distance"] = cdist(asked_scaled, surveyed_scaled).min(axis=1)
asked["far"] = asked["distance"] > limit
asked["every_range"] = np.logical_and.reduce([in_range(c) for c in inputs])

pd.DataFrame({
    "stations": [len(asked)],
    "inside every range": [asked["every_range"].sum()],
    "far from the survey": [asked["far"].sum()],
    "inside every range but far": [(asked["every_range"] & asked["far"]).sum()],
})
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: distance-numbers
#| include: false
n_range <- sum(asked$every_range)
n_hidden <- sum(asked$every_range & asked$far)
n_hidden_winter <- sum(asked$every_range & asked$far & asked$season == "winter")
```

Of the `r nrow(asked)` spring and winter stations, `r n_range` pass the range check
on every input. Yet `r n_hidden` of those, `r round(100 * n_hidden / n_range)`% of
the stations that pass, are far from every surveyed station, and
`r n_hidden_winter` of those are winter stations. @fig-novelty shows why. In summer
and autumn shallow water is warm, so the survey met cold water only at depth. Winter
cools the shallow water to temperatures the survey recorded, at depths it covered,
but never together.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-novelty
#| fig-cap: "Depth against temperature for the summer and autumn survey (grey) and the spring and winter stations its model is asked about. The dashed box is the survey's range of each input taken alone. Orange stations are inside every range yet far from any surveyed station; most are shallow and cold, a combination the survey did not meet, as its cold water was all deep."
#| fig-alt: "A scatter plot with depth from 0 to 200 metres on the horizontal axis and temperature from about 2 to 16 degrees on the vertical. Grey points, the summer and autumn survey, form a band that cools with depth, from about 10 to 16 degrees in shallow water to 6 to 11 degrees at 150 metres. A dashed box marks the survey's range of depth and temperature. Spring and winter stations are coloured: light blue ones, close to surveyed stations, sit along the lower edge of the grey band; dark blue ones, outside a range, lie mostly below the box, colder than any surveyed station, at depths beyond 90 metres; orange ones, inside every range but far from the survey, form a band beneath the grey points between the surface and about 100 metres, at 5 to 8 degrees, where the survey has no stations."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
novelty <- asked |>
  mutate(status = case_when(
    !every_range ~ "Outside a range",
    far ~ "Inside every range, far from the survey",
    .default = "Close to surveyed stations"
  ))

ggplot(mapping = aes(depth_m, temperature_c)) +
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = min(surveyed$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE),
           xmax = max(surveyed$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE),
           ymin = min(surveyed$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE),
           ymax = max(surveyed$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE),
           fill = NA, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = surveyed, colour = "grey75", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = status), data = novelty, size = 1.6,
             alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Close to surveyed stations" = ml_palette[["sky"]],
    "Outside a range" = ml_palette[["blue"]],
    "Inside every range, far from the survey" = ml_palette[["orange"]]
  )) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Temperature (°C)", colour = NULL)
```

:::

### The random forest's error grows with distance from the survey

A random forest fitted to the summer and autumn survey predicts the spring and winter
stations. Season itself is left out of its inputs, as the survey has none of the
seasons asked about. Its predictions are compared with the true mean count again, in
four groups of stations from the nearest quarter to the furthest. The error is the
factor a prediction is off by: one twice the truth and one half of it are both off by a
factor of 2.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: season-forest
season_forest <- workflow(
  recipe(abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 +
           salinity_psu + substrate, data = surveyed) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()),
  rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
    set_engine("ranger") |>
    set_mode("regression")
) |>
  fit(surveyed)

by_distance <- asked |>
  mutate(predicted = predict(season_forest, asked)$.pred) |>
  left_join(load_coastal_survey_truth(), by = "station_id") |>
  mutate(quarter = ntile(distance, 4),
         off_by = exp(abs(log(predicted / true_mean)))) |>
  summarise(stations = n(),
            `distance from` = min(distance), to = max(distance),
            `typical factor off` = median(off_by),
            .by = quarter) |>
  arrange(quarter)

by_distance |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
season_inputs = inputs + ["substrate"]
season_forest = Pipeline([
    ("recipe", ColumnTransformer([
        ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), inputs),
        ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["substrate"]),
    ])),
    ("model", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, random_state=1,
                                    n_jobs=-1)),
]).fit(surveyed[season_inputs], surveyed["abundance"])

by_distance = asked.assign(
    predicted=season_forest.predict(asked[season_inputs])
).merge(load_coastal_survey_truth(), on="station_id")
by_distance["quarter"] = pd.qcut(by_distance["distance"], 4, labels=[1, 2, 3, 4])
by_distance["off_by"] = np.exp(np.abs(np.log(by_distance["predicted"]
                                             / by_distance["true_mean"])))
(by_distance.groupby("quarter", observed=True)
 .agg(stations=("distance", "size"),
      distance_from=("distance", "min"), to=("distance", "max"),
      typical_factor_off=("off_by", "median"))
 .round(2).reset_index())
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: distance-error-numbers
#| include: false
off_near <- by_distance$`typical factor off`[1]
off_far <- by_distance$`typical factor off`[4]
```

At the quarter of stations nearest the survey, the forest is typically off by a
factor of `r round(off_near, 1)`. At the furthest quarter it is typically off by
`r round(off_far, 1)`. The forest reports nothing different at the far stations; the
distance is the only sign that its predictions there deserve less trust.

## The distance to the nearest station belongs on a prediction map

Mapped alongside a prediction, the distance to the nearest surveyed station shows
where the map rests on the survey and where it is extrapolating; areas far from the
survey can be greyed out or left unmapped.
[Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd)
measures a distance of the same kind on the map, to choose folds that hold stations as
far from the fitted data as the area to be mapped lies from the survey. When extrapolating is the point, as in projecting
a species' range under warmer water than any survey recorded, say which predictions are
extrapolations and expect errors larger than any cross-validation on the survey has
measured.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- A model answers for conditions its survey never covered, and nothing in its
  predictions shows that it has left the data.
- Methods that agree within the survey's range part company past it. Below 140 m the
  random forest stayed level and was too high on all ten shallow surveys, at
  `r spread_of("Random forest", "below")` times the true mean count; polynomial
  regression ranged from `r spread_of("Polynomial regression", "below")` times it.
- A range check on each input misses new combinations: of the `r n_range` spring and
  winter stations that passed it, `r n_hidden` were far from every surveyed station.
- The distance to the nearest surveyed station, on standardised inputs, flags such
  stations. The forest's typical error grew from a factor of `r round(off_near, 1)` at
  the nearest quarter of stations to `r round(off_far, 1)` at the furthest.
- Map that distance with the predictions, and treat areas far from the survey as
  extrapolation.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Refit the forest in `predict_two()` with `rand_forest(trees = 500, min_n = 50)`,
   so each leaf holds at least 50 stations, and redraw @fig-beyond. Does a smoother
   forest extrapolate any better?
2. Use `nearest()` to measure how far each deep station lies from the shallow
   survey, with both sets of stations prepared by a `distance_recipe` built on
   `shallow`. Do the stations deeper than 140 m stand out?
